metadata.summary: This joint guideline sets minimum standards for routine and sleep EEG recordings, including indications, technical specifications, recording duration, sleep induction and activation procedures. It presents 16 consensus-based recommendations developed from an evidence review and a modified Delphi process. The authors describe the overall research evidence as low quality and the recommendations as conditional.

conditions_covered: Epileptic encephalopathy with continuous spike-and-wave during sleep
self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood
target_population: Adults and children referred for routine or sleep EEG

toxicities.incidence: In category I studies of patients referred for EEG because epilepsy was suspected, seizures were provoked by hyperventilation in 2.2% (69/3170) and occurred exclusively during HV in 2.9% (25/877); 1/3170 patients had a generalized tonic clonic seizure. In a category II sample, seizures during hyperventilation appeared in 2.1% (12/580) of EEG reports.

management.actions: Assess the patient using a standardized seizure-testing method. For a possible absence seizure accompanying a generalized spike-and-wave discharge longer than 3-4 seconds, give simple instructions or words throughout the discharge, observe for a spontaneous response, and ask afterward what was said.

prevention: Explain the potential benefits and adverse effects of activation beforehand, including seizures and possible loss of driving permission; tell the patient that activation can be refused.
The EEG technician should continuously monitor one recording at a time and must not leave the patient alone.

Check for hyperventilation contraindications and document the patient's answers. These include sickle cell disease or trait, Moya-Moya disease and syndrome, cerebrovascular malformations including aneurysms, cerebrovascular events in the last three months, raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias and other severe cardiac disorders, severe pulmonary disorders, and pregnancy.

toxicities.incidence: Three category I studies observed psychogenic non-epileptic seizures during hyperventilation in 1.1% (10/877), 0.9% (31/3475), and none (0/326) of patients, respectively.
prevention: Inform patients about activation risks and their right to decline activation. A category III study found that telling patients about a possible seizure-inducing effect increased psychogenic non-epileptic seizures; the guideline nevertheless advises advance disclosure.

toxicities.incidence: A category I study reported seizures due to IPS in 0.72% (39/5383) of patients, including a generalized tonic clonic seizure in 0.04% of patients. Two category II studies reported seizures exclusively during IPS in 0.53% (1/189) and 0.68% (5/732) of patients. Among Air Force applicants, IPS caused epileptic seizures in 0.068% (4/5,893); three out of four were generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

management.actions: Use a standardized method to test the patient during the event.

prevention: Explain possible seizures, potential loss of driving permission, and the right to refuse activation before testing.
The EEG technician should continuously observe the patient and monitor one recording at a time.
Pregnancy is a contraindication to IPS because of the high seizure risk.

toxicities.event: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures during intermittent photic stimulation
toxicities.incidence: A category I study reported psychogenic non-epileptic seizures provoked by IPS in 0.9% (49/5383) of patients. In a category III study's informed group, 17.6% (6/34) had psychogenic non-epileptic seizures due to IPS; two thirds (4/6) occurred exclusively during IPS.
prevention: Tell patients about potential activation effects and their right to refuse. A category III study found a significantly higher rate of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures after patients were informed about possible seizure induction; this does not negate the guideline's advice to inform them.

toxicities.event: Perioral or finger numbness or tingling during hyperventilation
recognition: Numbness or tingling around the mouth or in the fingers may occur during hyperventilation.

management.actions: These symptoms alone are not a reason to stop hyperventilation.

toxicities.event: Cerebrovascular, cardiovascular or respiratory events during hyperventilation
toxicities.incidence: A category I safety study reported no significant cerebrovascular, cardiovascular or respiratory events.
prevention: Make the contraindication list available to the referring physician where possible. At a minimum, particularly when there is a delay between referral and EEG, the EEG technician should ask about contraindications and document the answer.

Hyperventilation is contraindicated with sickle cell disease or trait, Moya-Moya disease and syndrome, cerebrovascular malformations including aneurysms, a cerebrovascular event in the last three months, raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias or other severe cardiac disorders, severe pulmonary disorders, or pregnancy.

toxicities.event: Difficulty maintaining wakefulness at night or waking in the morning
toxicities.incidence: Difficulties keeping children awake at night or waking them in the morning occurred in 50% of patients in a cited study.
recognition: Difficulty keeping a child awake overnight or waking the child in the morning.

toxicities.event: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures coincident with sleep deprivation
toxicities.incidence: In two cited studies, generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred coincidentally with sleep deprivation in one patient.
prevention: The guideline notes that no studies have evaluated the safety of partial or full sleep deprivation in any age group.

toxicities.event: Potential cardiovascular adverse effects and central nervous system depression
toxicities.incidence: The frequency of adverse effects was higher with other sleep-inducing drugs than with melatonin; no numerical rate is given.
prevention: The guideline states that use of these drugs requires safety precautions but does not specify the precautions.

therapies_index.name: routine EEG
approved_indications: Non-emergent evaluation when a seizure or epilepsy is clinically suspected.
Reassessment of an epilepsy diagnosis, classification of an epilepsy syndrome, evaluation of a changed seizure pattern or investigation of epilepsy etiology.
Assessment before tapering AED in seizure-free patients and systematic follow-up of specified epilepsy syndromes.
Differential diagnosis involving psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, paroxysmal behavioral changes, suspected encephalopathy or acute or subacute dementia.
therapies_index.administration: The suggested recording duration is 20 min, with timing and duration individualized when greater diagnostic benefit is anticipated.
monitoring: A technician should continuously supervise one recording at a time and attend to patient safety and recording quality.

therapies_index.name: sleep EEG
approved_indications: A repeat EEG when another recording is needed.
Evaluation when artifacts leave little interpretable background in a routine awake recording, particularly in children.
Priority recording for suspected or diagnosed self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood or West syndrome.
therapies_index.administration: The suggested recording duration is 30 min. For infants and children, a postprandial appointment is advisable. When West syndrome is suspected, extending the recording for at least 10 minutes after awakening is suggested to improve the likelihood of capturing epileptic spasms.
monitoring: A technician should continuously supervise one recording at a time and attend to patient safety and recording quality.

therapies_index.name: partial sleep deprivation
approved_indications: Suggested as the primary method of inducing sleep for EEG in adults and children 12 years of age or older who can cooperate.
One of the suggested primary methods of inducing sleep for EEG in children under 12 years of age.
therapies_index.administration: For a morning sleep EEG, the suggested protocol varies by age: children aged < 6 year shorten sleep by 1-3 hours or by an amount judged sufficient to permit sleep during EEG; children aged 6-12 years go to bed two hours later and wake two hours earlier than usual, then remain awake until EEG; children aged > 12 years go to bed two hours later than usual, but no later than 00 AM, and remain awake from 04 AM until EEG; adults go to bed at 00 AM and remain awake after 04 AM until EEG.
key_toxicities: In one study, keeping children awake at night and waking them in the morning was difficult in 50% of patients.
The guideline notes that sleep deprivation may cause substantial distress for a child and family.

therapies_index.name: melatonin
approved_indications: Suggested as one of the primary methods of inducing sleep for EEG in children under 12 years of age.
Proposed as a primary sleep-induction method for children and adults unable to cooperate with partial sleep deprivation.
therapies_index.administration: The suggested dose is 1-3 mg, given 30-60 min before the start of EEG recording.

therapies_index.name: chloral hydrate
approved_indications: May be used to induce sleep for EEG when melatonin is unavailable and partial sleep deprivation has not achieved sleep.

therapies_index.name: hyperventilation
approved_indications: Suggested as an activation procedure during routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated.
therapies_index.administration: The patient takes 15-30 deep breaths /min for at least three minutes. In adults, it is suggested after intermittent photic stimulation, with at least 3 minutes between procedures; when the referral diagnosis is genetic generalized epilepsy, activations are advisable at the end of recording. In children undergoing sleep EEG, hyperventilation is suggested at the beginning. Recording two minutes of awake EEG afterward is preferable.
key_toxicities: Numbness or tingling around the mouth and in the fingers can occur and, by itself, is not a reason to stop.

In cited category I studies of patients referred for EEG because epilepsy was suspected, hyperventilation provoked seizures in 2.2% (69/3170) and seizures exclusively during hyperventilation in 2.9% (25/877).
Cited category I studies observed psychogenic non-epileptic seizures during hyperventilation in 1.1% (10/877) and 0.9% (31/3475) of patients.
monitoring: Check and document contraindications before the procedure.
The technician should assess whether breathing effort is adequate and maintain continuous patient supervision.
If a seizure occurs, testing with a standardized method is advisable.

therapies_index.name: intermittent photic stimulation
approved_indications: Suggested as an activation procedure during routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated.
therapies_index.administration: The guideline suggests following the cited ILAE photic-stimulation methodology. In adults, perform it before hyperventilation with at least 3 minutes between procedures; when the referral diagnosis is genetic generalized epilepsy, activations are advisable at the end of recording. For children undergoing sleep EEG, it is suggested at the end. Repetition within the same recording is unnecessary if the result is unequivocal.
key_toxicities: In a cited nationwide UK category I study, photic stimulation caused seizures in 0.72% (39/5383) of patients, including a generalized tonic clonic seizure in 0.04%, and provoked psychogenic non-epileptic seizures in 0.9% (49/5383).
monitoring: Check for pregnancy, which the guideline identifies as a contraindication.
Maintain continuous patient supervision and, if a seizure occurs, use a standardized testing method.

therapies_index.name: Asking the patient to blink, close and open eyes
approved_indications: Documentation of artifacts and assessment of eye-closure sensitivity during routine or sleep EEG.
therapies_index.administration: The summary recommends this at the beginning of routine EEG or during the waking period at the end of sleep EEG, when the posterior dominant rhythm can be assessed. Children may need help closing their eyes.

therapies_index.name: cognitive tasks
approved_indications: Discussed as a potential tailored provocation method for epilepsy with a reflex trait or a known seizure trigger; the guideline does not support routine use of provocation methods other than hyperventilation and intermittent photic stimulation.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited studies, cognitive-task protocols lasted at least 15 minutes and typically over 30 minutes.
key_toxicities: Seizures occurred during cognitive testing in three cited studies, whereas two cited studies did not observe them.

special_populations.considerations: Scheduling sleep EEG after a meal may make sleep more likely. In some children, artifacts can obscure so much of the awake recording that little undisturbed background remains; sleep EEG is recommended in that situation. The document notes that sleep deprivation can burden children and their families and that its safety has not been studied in any age group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Schedule sleep EEG in the postprandial period when appropriate. In children, perform hyperventilation at the beginning of sleep EEG and intermittent photic stimulation at the end.

special_populations.considerations: The suggested partial sleep deprivation protocol is intended for a morning sleep EEG.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Shorten sleep by 1-3 hours, or by an amount estimated to enable sleep during EEG.

special_populations.considerations: The document provides an age-specific partial sleep deprivation protocol for a morning sleep EEG.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Go to bed two hours later than usual, wake two hours earlier than usual, and remain awake until EEG.

special_populations.considerations: The suggested morning sleep EEG protocol specifies a different schedule from that for younger children.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Go to bed two hours later than usual, but no later than 00 AM, and remain awake from 04 AM until EEG.

special_populations.considerations: Either melatonin or sleep deprivation is suggested as the initial way to induce sleep. Combining them may work better if either method alone fails.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The suggested melatonin dose is 1-3 mg, given 30-60 min before EEG recording. If melatonin is unavailable and partial sleep deprivation does not produce sleep, chloral hydrate may be used.

special_populations.population: Adults and children ≥ 12 years of age who can cooperate with sleep deprivation
special_populations.considerations: Partial sleep deprivation is suggested as the primary sleep-induction method.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For adults undergoing morning sleep EEG, the suggested protocol is to go to bed at 00 AM and remain awake after 04 AM until EEG.

special_populations.population: Children and adults who cannot cooperate with partial sleep deprivation
special_populations.considerations: Melatonin is proposed as the primary sleep-induction method.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The suggested melatonin dose is 1-3 mg, administered 30-60 min before EEG recording.

special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy is listed as a contraindication to hyperventilation and, because of seizure risk, to intermittent photic stimulation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not perform these contraindicated activations.

special_populations.considerations: Listed contraindications are sickle cell disease or trait, Moya-Moya disease and syndrome, cerebrovascular malformations including aneurysms, cerebrovascular events in the last three months, raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias and other severe forms of cardiac disorders, and severe pulmonary disorders. The referring clinician should preferably have access to the contraindication list; at minimum, the EEG technician should ask about contraindications and document the response.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not perform hyperventilation when contraindicated.

special_populations.population: Patients with suspected juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
special_populations.considerations: A morning appointment may increase EEG yield.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider scheduling EEG in the morning.

special_populations.population: Patients with suspected or diagnosed self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood or West syndrome
special_populations.considerations: Prioritizing a sleep recording may increase EEG yield. When West syndrome is suspected, recording after awakening may improve the chance of capturing epileptic spasms.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Prioritize sleep EEG; for suspected West syndrome, extend recording at least 10 minutes after awakening.
conditions: self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood

special_populations.population: Patients referred with genetic generalized epilepsy
special_populations.considerations: Activations are more likely to provoke seizures in this group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Perform activations at the end of the recording rather than at the beginning.

conditions.name: epilepsy
conditions.description: The diagnosis is clinical. Scalp EEG contributes to diagnosis, syndrome classification and reassessment when the disorder evolves.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support assessment of suspected seizures or epilepsy, reconsider an initial diagnosis, classify the syndrome, and evaluate a changed seizure pattern or possible etiology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When epilepsy or a seizure is suspected, an established diagnosis needs reassessment, or the seizure pattern changes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interictal epileptiform discharges are relevant to diagnosis and classification; the sensitivity for detecting them increases with repeated recordings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Increase the opportunity to detect epileptiform discharges.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suggested for a repeat EEG and when artifacts make the awake background difficult to assess, particularly in children.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Epileptiform discharges occur more frequently during NREM sleep than during wakefulness. Most cited clinical studies suggest added diagnostic value over standard EEG, although some question its utility.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provoke epileptiform abnormalities or seizures during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an activation procedure during routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies found abnormalities absent from baseline EEG in some patients; the reported yield varies by study.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Elicit epileptiform abnormalities or seizures during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an activation procedure during routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies found generalized epileptiform discharges not seen before stimulation in some patients.

recommended_tests: EEG when epilepsy evolves or its diagnosis needs reassessment
EEG before tapering AED in seizure-free patients

subtypes.name: genetic generalized epilepsies with reflex trait
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Recognized as a group in which an established seizure trigger can justify tailored provocation during EEG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess activation of epileptiform discharges.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When EEG is requested for suspected genetic generalized epilepsy, the guideline advises placing activation procedures at the end of the recording because seizures may be more likely.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study found a significant increase in epileptiform discharge frequency relative to baseline in 23.7% (14/59) of patients.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity and epileptiform activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study found that type 4 accounted for 59% of photosensitivity reactions in genetic generalized epilepsy, compared with 38% in childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a known reflex trigger during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Considered when the task is known to provoke seizures; the guideline does not support routine use of provocation methods other than hyperventilation and IPS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies suggest that diagnostic yield may exceed that of hyperventilation and IPS, but not sleep.

conditions.name: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
conditions.clinical_presentation: The cited studies assessed myoclonia in this syndrome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Improve the likelihood of obtaining diagnostically useful findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is suspected, the guideline advises booking the recording in the morning.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate provocation of myoclonia or interictal epileptiform discharges.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Tailored use when a task is known to provoke seizures; routine use of additional provocation methods is not supported.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies found cognitive tasks more provocative of myoclonia than conventional methods in patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 50% of patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

conditions.name: self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Increase the likelihood of diagnostically useful EEG findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The guideline advises prioritizing sleep recording when this condition is suspected or diagnosed.

conditions.name: West syndrome
conditions.clinical_presentation: Epileptic spasms are a finding the guideline seeks to capture on EEG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Improve the likelihood of diagnostically useful findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The guideline advises prioritizing sleep recording when West syndrome is suspected or diagnosed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Increase the probability of recording epileptic spasms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When West syndrome is suspected, the guideline advises continuing the recording for at least 10 minutes after awakening.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline lists West syndrome as an example of a syndrome for which systematic EEG follow-up is indicated, without specifying a schedule.

conditions.name: Epileptic encephalopathy with continuous spike-and-wave during sleep

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline names this syndrome as an example warranting systematic EEG follow-up but gives no interval.

conditions.name: focal-onset epilepsies with a specific seizure trigger
conditions.description: These epilepsies have a particular trigger that can guide individualized EEG activation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Attempt to elicit a seizure using an established trigger.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a stimulus is known to provoke the patient's seizures; the guideline does not support routine use of additional provocation methods.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated as a possible provocation method.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited study did not find increased diagnostic utility from olfactory stimulation; the guideline does not support its routine use.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 23% of patients with childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes. In the same study, type 4 represented 38% of photosensitivity reactions in childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes, compared with 59% in genetic generalized epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 56% of patients with juvenile absence epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 44% of patients with childhood absence epilepsy.

conditions.name: epilepsy with generalized tonic clonic seizures on awakening
conditions.clinical_presentation: The syndrome is characterized in the document by generalized tonic clonic seizures occurring on awakening.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 74% of patients with epilepsy with generalized tonic clonic seizures on awakening.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess photosensitivity during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an EEG activation procedure unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 16% of patients with symptomatic/cryptogenic epilepsy.

conditions.name: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures
conditions.description: The guideline treats these events as an indication for differential diagnosis with EEG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to differential diagnosis of suspected psychogenic non-epileptic seizures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When these events are suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Observe whether activation elicits an event during EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As activation procedures unless contraindicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies observed psychogenic non-epileptic seizures during activation. One cited category III study found more such events when patients were told that activation might induce a seizure.

conditions.name: Suspected encephalopathy
conditions.description: Listed as an indication for non-emergent EEG in differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When encephalopathy is suspected.

conditions.name: Acute or subacute dementia
conditions.description: Listed as an indication for non-emergent EEG in differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In the setting of acute or subacute dementia.

artifacts.description: The table sets out the clinical questions and their PICO elements. Technical standards are identified as not practically applicable to that framework.
artifacts.summary: Defines the questions used to examine EEG indications, technical standards, provocation, recording duration and sleep induction.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Clarifies which populations, interventions, comparisons and outcomes informed the guideline’s assessment.

artifacts.title: Table 2. Indications of non-emergent EEG recorded by appointment

artifacts.description: The indications reflect a consensus-based weak (conditional) recommendation; the guideline reports no eligible research evidence establishing indications for routine and sleep EEG.
artifacts.summary: Groups appointment-based, non-emergent EEG indications into epilepsy-related uses and other differential-diagnostic uses.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps clinicians decide when a non-emergent EEG referral may be appropriate without treating the listed indications as strongly evidence-based.

artifacts.description: The table spans multiple groups of standards and has no explicit column headings. The continuation about performing HV at the end of recording follows the genetic generalized epilepsy exception. Its layout separates this continuation from the preceding cell; the prose specifies that the exception applies when the referral diagnosis is genetic generalized epilepsy. The asterisk cites the ILAE photic-stimulation methodology publication. The guideline describes its minimum-standard recommendations as conditional.
artifacts.summary: Brings together electrode and recording specifications, minimum durations, sleep-induction approaches and activation procedures for routine and sleep EEG.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Provides operational parameters for EEG acquisition and highlights situations requiring changes to the usual timing or method of recording.

artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports age-specific preparation when partial sleep deprivation is selected to increase the chance of recording sleep.

artifacts.clinical_relevance: Promotes consistent documentation of responsiveness, motor actions, recall and the patient’s account of an event.

recommendations.statement: If another EEG is needed, perform a sleep EEG for the repeat recording.
recommendations.context: Repeat assessment after an initial EEG.
recommendations.rationale: Repeated recordings increase sensitivity for epileptiform discharges, which occur more frequently during NREM sleep than during wakefulness.

recommendations.statement: Perform a sleep EEG when artifacts obscure so much of the routine waking recording that little uninterrupted background activity can be assessed.
recommendations.context: This problem is particularly relevant in children.

recommendations.statement: Consider an EEG scheduled outside an emergency setting for suspected seizure or epilepsy, reassessment of an epilepsy diagnosis, epilepsy syndrome classification, a changed seizure pattern, etiological assessment of epilepsy, evaluation before tapering AED in seizure-free patients, or systematic follow-up of selected epilepsy syndromes such as West syndrome and Epileptic encephalopathy with continuous spike-and-wave during sleep.
recommendations.rationale: The working group found no eligible research evidence establishing indications for routine or sleep EEG and reached consensus through modified Delphi discussions.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1.1 Recommendation; Table 2. Indications of non-emergent EEG recorded by appointment

recommendations.statement: Consider an EEG scheduled outside an emergency setting to help differentiate psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, paroxysmal behavioral changes, suspected encephalopathy, or acute or subacute dementia.
recommendations.rationale: The indication list reflects modified Delphi consensus rather than eligible research evidence on EEG indications.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1.1 Recommendation; Table 2. Indications of non-emergent EEG recorded by appointment

recommendations.statement: For routine EEG, use individually applied gold or silver/silver-chloride cup electrodes with electrode paste or gel.
recommendations.rationale: The technical standards were developed by consensus because the available evidence was of low quality.

recommendations.statement: Electrode caps are acceptable if electrode impedances are checked and satisfy the recommended standards.
Do not yet use dry electrode EEG systems as a recommended recording method.
recommendations.rationale: These systems produce more movement and sweat artifacts, while approaches intended to reduce those artifacts have not been adequately studied.

recommendations.statement: MRI compatible electrodes or needle electrodes may be used in appropriate circumstances.
Use the 25 electrode IFCN montage whenever feasible; otherwise, the 10-20 array is acceptable.
recommendations.rationale: Adding subtemporal electrodes improves detection of ictal and interictal epileptiform discharges.

recommendations.statement: One ECG channel may be recorded alongside EEG.
Record at least two EMG channels when clinically relevant motor events are suspected.
recommendations.rationale: Bilateral extremity EMG can objectively document movement for correlation with EEG and help characterize motor seizure features.

recommendations.statement: When eye movement artifacts are difficult to distinguish from slow EEG activity, two EOG leads may be placed: one cm lateral and above the right outer canthus and one cm lateral and below the left outer canthus.
recommendations.context: Polygraphic channels and EOG lead placement.

recommendations.statement: Check scalp-electrode impedance at the start of each EEG recording.
recommendations.rationale: An impedance below 100 Ω is unacceptable because it often indicates a salt bridge on the scalp.

recommendations.statement: Aim for scalp-electrode impedances below 5 kΩ; an impedance of less than 10 kΩ remains acceptable.
recommendations.rationale: Higher or uneven impedances can increase artifacts and impair common mode rejection.

recommendations.statement: Use a minimum EEG sampling rate of 256 Hz.
recommendations.rationale: The proposed rate reflects expert experience and the frequency content of clinically relevant EEG signals.

recommendations.statement: For EEG visualization, use a suggested high-pass filter setting of 0.5 Hz and low-pass filter setting of 70 Hz.
Use the proposed display resolution of 7 µV/mm for adult EEG; for children, use the suggested resolution of 10 µV/mm.

Allow EEG reviewers to adjust individual channel gain, time resolution, annotations, and low-pass and high-pass filters; they should also be able to display voltage maps at a selected time point and apply notch filters.
Archive the complete EEG recording and time-synchronized video, either throughout the recording or at least for clinically relevant events.
Enable export of EEG data for research in Comma Separated Values (CSV) or European Data Format (EDF).
recommendations.context: Data export; Table 3 additionally lists Digital Communication in Medicine (DICOM) as a format, while the accompanying text describes its development as ongoing.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.2.4 Data storage and export; Table 3. Summary of minimum standards for recording routine and sleep EEG

recommendations.statement: Use a recording duration of 20 minutes for routine EEG.
recommendations.rationale: The recommendation was reached by modified Delphi consensus because evidence on optimal duration was of low quality.

recommendations.statement: Use a recording duration of 30 minutes for sleep EEG.
recommendations.rationale: The recommendation was reached by modified Delphi consensus because evidence on optimal duration was of low quality.

recommendations.statement: Schedule sleep EEG for infants and children in the postprandial period when practicable.
recommendations.rationale: Falling asleep is more likely after a meal.

recommendations.statement: Individualize EEG scheduling and recording duration when a greater diagnostic benefit is anticipated.
recommendations.context: Adjustment of routine or sleep EEG scheduling and duration.

recommendations.statement: Consider a morning EEG appointment for a patient with suspected juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
recommendations.rationale: This timing probably improves EEG yield.

recommendations.statement: Prioritize a sleep recording when self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood or West syndrome is suspected or diagnosed.
recommendations.rationale: A sleep recording probably improves EEG yield in these circumstances.

recommendations.statement: When West syndrome is suspected, continue recording for at least 10 minutes after awakening.
recommendations.context: Sleep EEG recording duration after waking.
recommendations.rationale: This extension probably increases the likelihood of capturing epileptic spasms.

recommendations.statement: Use partial sleep deprivation as the primary sleep-induction method for adults and for children 12 years of age or older who can cooperate with it.
recommendations.rationale: Partial sleep deprivation increases the likelihood of sleep during EEG and is feasible without medication-administration resources. The document notes that its safety has not been studied for any age group and that it may distress children and families.

recommendations.statement: Use either melatonin or sleep deprivation as a primary method of inducing sleep in children under 12 years of age.
recommendations.context: Sleep induction for pediatric EEG; the document rates evidence for pharmacological sleep induction as very low.
recommendations.rationale: Pediatric studies examined both methods, but the evidence for pharmacological induction has substantial limitations.

recommendations.statement: If either melatonin or sleep deprivation alone does not induce sleep, consider using them together.
recommendations.context: Sleep induction after failure of an initial method.
recommendations.rationale: Their combination may be more effective for inducing sleep.

recommendations.statement: Use melatonin as a primary sleep-induction method for children or adults unable to cooperate with partial sleep deprivation.
recommendations.context: Sleep induction when cooperation with sleep deprivation is not possible.
recommendations.rationale: The document identifies serious limitations and imprecision in evidence on pharmacological sleep induction.

recommendations.statement: When using melatonin for sleep induction, administer 1-3 mg 30-60 min before the EEG recording begins.
If melatonin is unavailable, chloral hydrate may be used when partial sleep deprivation has failed to produce sleep.
recommendations.rationale: Other sleep-inducing drugs had more frequent adverse effects than melatonin and required precautions for possible cardiovascular effects and central nervous system depression.

recommendations.statement: Include hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and baseline recording with eyes open and eyes closed in routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated.
recommendations.context: Routine activation methods; the document rates evidence for hyperventilation as moderate and for photic stimulation as low.
recommendations.rationale: Hyperventilation and photic stimulation can reveal epileptiform abnormalities absent from baseline recordings.

recommendations.statement: Ask the patient to blink and to close and open the eyes during EEG recording.
recommendations.context: Table 3 places this assessment at the beginning of routine EEG or during the waking period at the end of sleep EEG; children may need assistance with eye closure.
recommendations.rationale: These actions document artifacts and can provoke eye-closure sensitivity; assessment after sleep also permits evaluation of the posterior dominant rhythm.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.4 Recommendation; Table 3. Summary of minimum standards for recording routine and sleep EEG

recommendations.statement: Tailor the EEG and consider simple additional stimuli, such as touch, sudden noises, or reading a difficult passage aloud, when they are known to provoke the patient's seizures.
recommendations.context: Individualized provocation rather than standard use of additional methods.
recommendations.rationale: The document found no evidence supporting routine use of provocation methods other than hyperventilation and intermittent photic stimulation.

recommendations.statement: Inform the patient and caregiver before activation procedures about possible benefits and adverse effects, especially seizures and possible loss of driving permission, and explain that the patient may decline activation.
recommendations.context: Consent and counseling before EEG activation.
recommendations.rationale: Information about seizure induction may itself increase the occurrence of non-epileptic seizures.

recommendations.statement: Have the EEG technician continuously monitor one recording at a time; do not leave the patient alone, and do not rely on a parent or guardian as the sole observer for more than a few minutes.
recommendations.context: Patient safety and recording quality during EEG.

recommendations.statement: During a seizure captured on routine or sleep EEG, assess the patient with a standardized approach adapted to age, including responsiveness and motor commands, followed by questions about the event after it ends.
recommendations.context: Table 5 provides suggested procedures for children < 6 years old and for children ≥ 6 years old and adults; the latter procedure also assesses repetition and later recall of words.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.4 Recommendation; Table 5. Suggested protocol for testing patients during seizures in routine and sleep EEG

recommendations.statement: For a possible absence seizure associated with a generalized spike-and-wave discharge lasting longer than 3-4 seconds, give simple instructions or words from the start of the discharge and throughout the absence, observe for a spontaneous response, and after the discharge ask the patient what was said.
recommendations.context: Assessment during a possible absence seizure.

recommendations.statement: In adults, perform intermittent photic stimulation before hyperventilation near the beginning of EEG, separating the procedures by at least 3 minutes.
recommendations.context: Order of adult EEG activations when the referral diagnosis does not require a different order.

recommendations.statement: If the referral diagnosis is genetic generalized epilepsy, perform activation procedures at the end of the recording.
recommendations.context: Exception to the usual activation order.
recommendations.rationale: The document identifies an increased likelihood of seizures in this setting.

recommendations.statement: For children undergoing sleep EEG, perform hyperventilation at the start and intermittent photic stimulation at the end.
recommendations.context: Order of pediatric sleep EEG activations.
recommendations.rationale: Intermittent photic stimulation often increases alertness and reduces the chance of sleep, whereas hyperventilation has the opposite effect.

recommendations.statement: For hyperventilation, instruct the patient to take deep breaths at a rate of 15-30 times/minute for at least three minutes; encourage the effort and assess whether breathing is adequate.
recommendations.context: Hyperventilation protocol; a windmill can help children breathe as instructed.

recommendations.statement: Preferably record two minutes of awake EEG after hyperventilation in all patient groups.

Do not perform hyperventilation when the patient has sickle cell disease or trait, Moya-Moya disease and syndrome, cerebrovascular malformations including aneurysms, a cerebrovascular event in the last three months, raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias or other severe cardiac disorders, severe pulmonary disorders, or pregnancy.

Preferably make the hyperventilation contraindication list available to the referring physician; at a minimum, the EEG technician should ask the patient about contraindications and document the response, particularly if time has elapsed since referral.
Perform intermittent photic stimulation according to the ILAE guideline on revisited methodology of photic stimulation in EEG recording.
Do not repeat intermittent photic stimulation within the same EEG recording if its result is unequivocal.
Do not perform intermittent photic stimulation during pregnancy.
recommendations.rationale: The document attributes this contraindication to a high risk of seizure.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: This joint ILAE and IFCN guideline sets minimum standards for routine and sleep EEG. Its working group followed the ILAE approach to epilepsy-related guidelines and reviewed published research using PRISMA. GRADE was used to assess sleep-induction evidence and formulate recommendations; QUADAS-2 assessed bias in technical and methodological studies. Where adequate evidence was unavailable, a modified Delphi process established expert agreement. Evidence quality was low or moderate. The document presents 16 consensus-based recommendations addressing indications, technical requirements, recording length, sleep induction, and activation procedures.

document_sections.heading: Key points
document_sections.content: Minimum standards are intended to improve the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of routine and sleep EEG. An ILAE–IFCN working group developed them. Research evidence was generally of low quality, so the recommendations are conditional. Further high-quality studies of EEG methods and diagnostic accuracy are needed.

document_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
document_sections.content: Non-invasive EEG remains important for assessing brain electrical activity in epilepsy and selected disorders of brain function. Epilepsy is defined clinically, but scalp EEG contributes to diagnosis, follow-up when the condition changes, and syndrome classification. An ILAE task force distinguished basic EEG recording, which includes routine EEG and activation procedures, from advanced recording, which uses sleep induction. Epileptiform discharges occur more frequently during NREM sleep than wakefulness. Most clinical studies suggest additional diagnostic value from sleep EEG, although some question it. Repeated EEG increases sensitivity for epileptiform discharges; when a recording is repeated, sleep EEG is recommended on the second occasion. Sleep EEG is also recommended when artifacts, particularly in children, obscure most of the awake background. Technical standards seek consistent laboratory quality and can be adapted across countries and healthcare levels. Earlier European ILAE recommendations appeared in 2002 without subsequent updating. A 2017 survey of 28 ERN EpiCARE members found that nearly every center used local EEG guidance. Inconsistent routine EEG standards also hinder multicenter research, as noted in Human Epilepsy Project 1; that observation was unpublished. American, Canadian, and French organizations have issued newer national guidance, but the absence of comprehensive international guidance obstructs global good-practice standards. The ILAE and IFCN therefore initiated this joint work. The ILAE Guidelines Task Force approved its protocol, which followed ILAE guideline-development methods and PRISMA. Intended readers are healthcare staff who refer patients, acquire recordings, interpret EEG, or prepare reports.

document_sections.heading: 2 Methods
document_sections.content: The methods comprise working-group formation, clinical-question development, literature searching, study selection, evidence appraisal, and consensus-based recommendation development.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Establishing a working group
document_sections.content: The ILAE and IFCN appointed members to a group of ten adult and pediatric neurologists specializing in epileptology and clinical neurophysiologists. Members came from four of six WHO regions. The ILAE Guidelines Task Force approved the group.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Developing clinical questions
document_sections.content: Five subgroups, each with 2-3 members, examined five clinical questions. PICO structured questions when applicable; Table 1 sets out the questions and their PICO elements.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Search strategy
document_sections.content: A PRISMA-based electronic search covered English-language publications in PubMed and EMBASE between 1990 and September-December 2019. Appendix 2 contains the complete PubMed searches and final access dates. The five search topics concerned indications and referrals for routine, sleep, and outpatient EEG; technical and minimum recording standards; recording duration and diagnostic yield; sleep deprivation, melatonin, and other sleep-induction methods; and hyperventilation, photic stimulation, eye closure, triggers, and other activation methods.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 Study selection, data extraction and synthesis of results
document_sections.content: Eligibility criteria were tailored to each of the five questions. Neonatal EEG, emergency EEG, intensive-care monitoring, and long-term epilepsy monitoring were outside scope. For indications, eligible studies examined non-emergent EEG for diagnosis or follow-up; randomized trials were sought, and other utility studies required an appropriate no-EEG control and follow-up measures of effects on care. Technical studies could address electrode arrays and montages, impedance, synchronized video, sampling and frequency characteristics, ancillary equipment, display, storage, and data formats. Duration studies compared recording lengths using EEG abnormalities as the primary outcome and cost-benefit as a secondary outcome. Sleep-induction studies compared 24h or partial deprivation with no deprivation, pharmacological induction, or other drugs; sleep occurrence was the outcome, with adverse effects and cost-benefit secondary. Studies of activation methods other than sleep assessed epileptiform abnormalities, epileptic seizures, or psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, and secondarily adverse effects. At least two subgroup members independently screened titles and abstracts; reference lists were checked. Two independent reviewers assessed full texts. Data-extraction procedures differed by question.

document_sections.heading: 2.5 Quality rating of individual studies and synthesis of results
document_sections.content: GRADE assessed bias in pharmacological and non-pharmacological sleep-induction intervention studies. QUADAS-2 assessed other, noninterventional studies because its diagnostic-accuracy domains addressed relevant technical and methodological limitations, although those studies were not themselves diagnostic-accuracy studies. Two reviewers resolved appraisal disagreements through discussion. Studies were classified as meta-analyses, systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials (RCT), observational studies including diagnostic-accuracy studies, case series, or guidelines. Given limited high-level evidence, observational studies received additional predefined categories: Category I covered large (N>50) prospective broad-spectrum studies and large blinded technical studies with an acceptable gold standard; Category II covered large prospective narrow-spectrum studies, large retrospective broad-spectrum studies, and small (N=10 – 50) blinded technical studies with an acceptable gold standard; Category III covered large retrospective narrow-spectrum studies, small prospective or retrospective studies, and unblinded technical studies or those lacking an acceptable reference standard; Category IV covered mathematical simulations. Study heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis, so synthesis was qualitative.

document_sections.heading: 2.6 Methods of recommendation
document_sections.content: GRADE assessed overall evidence for sleep-induction approaches and sleep yield during EEG. Other questions were assessed using individual studies’ bias ratings, classifications, and categories. Because overall evidence quality was low, subgroups used a modified Delphi process: anonymous written questionnaires were followed by open discussions, with rounds continuing until at least 2/3 of members agreed. For each subgroup, one member prepared questions and supporting literature analysis, did not answer the questionnaire, analyzed responses, and chaired an online consensus meeting. Recommendation strength followed the ILAE guideline-development guidance.

document_sections.heading: 3 Results
document_sections.content: Results address EEG indications, technical standards, recording duration, sleep induction, and provocative procedures.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Indications of routine and sleep EEG
document_sections.content: The database search identified 121 articles and other sources added six. After deduplication, 99 abstracts were screened; fourteen full texts underwent eligibility review. Three guidelines were included, but none of the 11 research studies qualified because their design and methods could not establish indications for routine or sleep EEG. The screened studies instead described EEG findings in particular illnesses. Earlier consensus guidelines for adults and children emphasize suspected epilepsy as the principal indication. More recent clinical summaries discuss EEG in seizure and epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring, the sensitivity and specificity of interictal epileptiform discharges, the value of awake and sleep recordings for epilepsy diagnosis and classification, and EEG’s role in decisions about antiseizure medication withdrawal.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1 Recommendation
document_sections.content: The group found no evidence establishing indications for routine or sleep EEG. Modified Delphi agreement nevertheless supports a weak (conditional) recommendation for indications for non-emergent EEG scheduled by appointment; Table 2 lists them.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Technical standards
document_sections.content: The search yielded eighteen articles, with 14 more from other sources. Following deduplication, 30 abstracts were assessed and ten full texts entered qualitative synthesis: four guidelines and six Category III observational studies. Individual studies had low risk of bias, but their lower observational category and heterogeneous outcomes reduced evidence quality. Earlier guidelines had based technical standards on expert judgment rather than scientific studies. The group rates evidence for technical standards as low and its modified-Delphi consensus recommendation as conditional. Table 3 summarizes the standards.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1 Electrodes and montages
document_sections.content: For routine EEG, individually placed gold or silver/silver-chloride cup electrodes with paste or gel are suggested. Electrode caps are also acceptable when impedances are measured and meet standards. Dry electrode systems are not yet recommended: movement and sweat artifacts are more frequent, and proposed mitigation methods, including automated artifact removal, lack thorough evaluation. MRI-compatible and needle electrodes are acceptable in particular circumstances. Use of the 25 electrode IFCN montage, adding six subtemporal electrodes to the 10-20 array, is suggested wherever feasible because studies indicate improved detection of ictal and interictal epileptiform discharges; otherwise, the 10-20 array is acceptable. One ECG channel may be used. At least two EMG channels are suggested when clinically relevant motor events are suspected. Bilateral limb EMG provides movement measurements that can be related to EEG, helping characterize myoclonus, spasms, clonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures and distinguish tonic from atonic seizures. Two EOG leads may help separate eye-movement artifacts from slow EEG activity. When used, recommended positions are one cm lateral and above the right outer canthus and one cm lateral and below the left outer canthus.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2 Electrode impedances
document_sections.content: Checking scalp-electrode impedance at the start of every recording is advisable. Values below 100 Ω are unacceptable because they commonly indicate scalp salt-bridge shunting. Skin abrasion generally remains necessary to limit interference and achieve less than 5 kΩ, although it is not proposed in a small subset of cases. Some evidence suggests 10 kΩ or higher can be acceptable with modern high-input-impedance amplifiers, but those studies examined only signal amplitude, 60 Hz artifact amplitude, and evoked-potential resolution; expert assessments of EEG signal quality at different impedances are lacking. Higher impedance may increase sweat, movement, and electrode-pop artifacts. Allowing values up to 10 kΩ also increases the likelihood of uneven impedances across electrodes, potentially weakening common-mode rejection. Consequently, below 5 kΩ is suggested, while less than 10 kΩ is considered acceptable.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3 Recording and review settings
document_sections.content: Frequencies over 100 Hz are not presently regarded as clinically relevant to routine EEG, although future artifact-reduction systems using blind source separation may benefit from higher-frequency data. Under the Nyquist theorem, the highest measurable frequency is half the sampling rate: 256 sample/sec (Hz) corresponds to 128 Hz. In practice, phase alignment requires sampling at least 2.5 times the signal’s highest frequency component. Expert experience and clinically relevant EEG frequencies underpin a proposed minimum sampling rate of 256 Hz. Suggested display filters are low-pass 70 Hz and high-pass 0.5 Hz. Proposed display resolution is 7 µV/mm, or 10 µV/mm for children. Reviewers should be able to change channel gains individually, alter time resolution, view voltage maps at a selected time, edit annotations, apply notch filters, and adjust low-pass and high-pass filters when needed.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4 Data storage and export
document_sections.content: Archiving the full EEG is suggested, together with synchronized video of either the entire session or clinically relevant events. Users are recommended to have research-export capability in Comma Separated Values (CSV) or European Data Format (EDF). IFCN is collaborating on a Digital Communication in Medicine (DICOM) format for EEG storage and exchange, expected to become available within the next few years.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Duration of recording
document_sections.content: Searches produced 156 database articles and 19 additional articles. After duplicates were removed, 152 abstracts were screened, Forty-one full texts assessed, and twelve articles included in qualitative analysis; three were EEG-recording guidelines. Nine eligible original studies comprised two category I studies and seven category IIIII observational studies. Only two Category II studies evaluated sleep-EEG duration. Every study had QUADAS-2 domains at high risk of bias, most often involving the reference standard. Earlier ILAE, American, and Canadian consensus guidelines recommended at least 20 minutes of technically satisfactory routine EEG; one recommended 30 minutes for sleep EEG. In a category I study of children and adults, 15 min routine EEG versus 25 minute-EEG had 94.1% [CI:88.7-97.4%] sensitivity and 99.3% [CI:97.5 -99.9%] specificity for epileptiform or non-epileptiform abnormalities. Sensitivity restricted to epileptiform abnormalities was 97.1% [CI: 92.6-99.2%]. Those authors judged 15-minute routine EEG potentially cost-effective if activation procedures were rigorously included. A category II pediatric study estimated that reducing routine EEG from 20 to 15 minutes could miss epileptiform abnormalities in 2.36% [CI: 0.63–4.09%] of recordings. The largest category II retrospective study, conducted at a tertiary epilepsy center, found significantly lower diagnostic yield below 20 minutes, but no significant yield difference between 20 and 30-minute routine recordings or between 30 and 60-minute sleep recordings in adults. Another category I study found that, for 4.5% of patients (81/1803), interictal epileptiform abnormalities first appeared after the initial 30 minutes; relative yield increased by 19.1% [CI: 15.6–23%]. A category II study found an 11% (p=0.001) increase in epileptiform-abnormality yield when recording length increased from 20 to 40 minutes. Another category II study detected 51% of epileptiform abnormalities within 20 minutes of sleep-deprived EEG, 71% within 30 minutes, and 93% within 90 minutes.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1 Recommendation
document_sections.content: Evidence on optimal routine- and sleep-EEG duration is low quality; the recommendations are therefore conditional. Modified Delphi consensus suggests 20 minutes for routine EEG and 30 minutes for sleep EEG. Scheduling infant and child sleep EEG after a meal is advisable because sleep is more likely then. Recording timing and duration should be individualized when greater benefit is anticipated. Morning appointments for suspected juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, prioritizing sleep recordings for suspected or established self-limited focal onset epilepsy of childhood or West syndrome, and continuing at least 10 minutes after awakening when West syndrome is suspected probably increase EEG yield by improving the chance of capturing epileptic spasms.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Sleep inducing methods
document_sections.content: Searches located 360 database articles and 20 additional articles. After deduplication, 259 records were screened; sixty-nine full texts underwent eligibility review. Seventeen studies met criteria, including three guidelines. All but one study assessed sleep induction in children or young adults up to 18 years of age. Earlier EEG guidelines did not specify an adult induction method; for children they recommended natural sleep, with partial deprivation or melatonin if natural sleep failed. One RCT affected by indirectness and three category II observational studies without serious limitations compared partial deprivation against no deprivation in children and young adults. WHO regions were not all represented, and the burden on patients, families, and society is likely culturally dependent. No study used stressful 24h deprivation. Ten studies—six RCTs and four observational studies, all at high risk of bias—examined melatonin or another drug. Their findings were inconsistent and imprecise because methods varied and study numbers and sample sizes were often small. Publication bias was considered possible for 24h deprivation and sedative drugs other than melatonin, commonly used before 1990 but subsequently abandoned because of adverse effects. Studies did not directly compare induction methods’ cost-benefit; sleep-onset latency could only serve as an indirect efficiency measure. Nine drug studies reported adverse effects, but had serious limitations.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1 Efficiency of sleep induction
document_sections.content: Studies showed that partial sleep deprivation increased the likelihood of obtaining sleep during EEG. One category I and one category II study found melatonin and partial deprivation equally effective for inducing sleep in pediatric patients, without different interictal epileptiform-discharge yields. A category II study suggested that melatonin might work better at ages 1-4 years than in older children. A multicenter category I study found combined deprivation and melatonin significantly more effective for inducing sleep than either alone, whereas a smaller category I study found no improvement in sleep latency from their combination. None of the included studies found an intergroup difference in epileptiform-abnormality yield. Melatonin doses in studies ranged from 2 mg to 10 mg; no trial assessed dose dependence for acute hypnotic or anxiolytic use in children. In healthy young adults, increasing the dose from 1.0 to 10 mg did not significantly shorten sleep-onset latency or increase subjective sleepiness. A separate European pediatric-neurology consensus suggested 1-3 mg 30 min before examination. When potential benefit is weighed against adverse effects, evidence does not establish an advantage for other sleep-inducing drugs over melatonin.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2 Adverse effects and tolerability
document_sections.content: Category I observational studies and randomized trials that systematically monitored pediatric adverse effects did not identify significant melatonin-related effects. Other sleep-inducing drugs had more frequent adverse effects and required precautions for possible cardiovascular effects and central nervous system depression. With sleep deprivation, difficulty keeping children awake overnight or waking them in the morning occurred in 50% of patients in one study. In two studies, generalized tonic-clonic seizures coincided with deprivation in one patient in each study.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3 Cost-effectiveness
document_sections.content: One category I study reported significantly shorter sleep latency with melatonin (mean latency 21 min) than with partial deprivation (mean latency 34 min); another category I study did not confirm this. A category I study also found significantly shorter latency when melatonin and partial deprivation were combined than with either method separately.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.4 Recommendation
document_sections.content: Evidence that partial deprivation induces sleep during EEG is moderate for children and young adults. Evidence for pharmacological induction is very low because of study limitations, few studies, small samples, and adverse effects. Partial sleep deprivation is suggested as the first sleep-induction approach for adults and children 12 years of age or older who can cooperate. It can be used irrespective of drug availability or personnel for drug administration. Table 4 provides a suggested protocol, but no study has evaluated the safety of partial or complete deprivation at any age; deprivation may substantially distress a child and family. For children under 12 years, either melatonin or deprivation is suggested initially. If either fails, combining them may work better. Melatonin is also proposed initially for children and adults unable to cooperate with partial deprivation. The suggested melatonin dose is 1-3 mg, given 30-60 min before EEG begins. If melatonin is unavailable and partial deprivation does not produce sleep, chloral hydrate may be used.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Provocative methods
document_sections.content: Searches identified 3483 database records and 13 articles elsewhere. After deduplication, 3049 abstracts were screened and one hundred twenty-eight full texts assessed. Forty-two original studies and four guidelines entered review. Eighteen observational studies assessed hyperventilation, 24 assessed intermittent photic stimulation (IPS), and nine compared other activation methods with IPS, hyperventilation, or sleep; some examined multiple methods. Every study had high risk of bias owing to limitations in both index and reference tests.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1 Hyperventilation
document_sections.content: The reviewed evidence addresses hyperventilation procedures, additional diagnostic yield, and safety.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1.1 Protocol and technical standards
document_sections.content: Only two studies evaluated the hyperventilation protocol. In a category I study, the final 2 min of 5 min of hyperventilation accounted for 16% of provoked seizures, 30.4% of interictal EEG abnormalities, and 30% of epileptiform discharges. Conversely, a category III study found 85.5% of absence seizures were induced within 1.5 min. Earlier EEG guidelines recommended at least three minutes, with prolongation or repetition when typical absence seizures were strongly suspected.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1.2 Yield of hyperventilation
document_sections.content: Three large category I studies found additional diagnostic value: hyperventilation revealed epileptiform abnormalities absent from baseline EEG in 0.92% (3/326), 1.1% (10/877), or 3.0% (95/3170) of adult and pediatric patients. Two Category II studies found abnormalities solely during hyperventilation in 0.86% (5/580) and 5.7% (8/141) of patients. In a category III newly diagnosed epilepsy cohort, abnormalities absent at baseline were provoked in 7.7% (25/325), with the highest yield at ages 1-19 years (10.3%). Hyperventilation elicited no epileptiform activity in a study of 100 healthy young men. A category III study found a significant increase over baseline in epileptiform-discharge frequency in 23.7% (14/59) of patients with genetic generalized epilepsy.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1.3 Safety
document_sections.content: A category I safety study found no significant cerebrovascular, cardiovascular, or respiratory events. Provoked seizures were relatively uncommon. Two category I studies reported hyperventilation-provoked seizures in 2.2% (69/3170), and seizures exclusively during HV in 2.9% (25/877), among patients referred for suspected epilepsy. Only 1/3170 had a generalized tonic clonic seizure. A category II sample of 580 routine-EEG reports recorded hyperventilation-provoked seizures in 2.1% (12/580); smaller category II and III studies, including genetic generalized epilepsy cohorts, reported similar or lower rates. Three category I studies recorded psychogenic non-epileptic seizures during hyperventilation in 1.1% (10/877), 0.9% (31/3475), and none (0/326), respectively. A category III study found more such seizures when patients had been told that hyperventilation might induce a seizure.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2 Intermittent photic stimulation
document_sections.content: The reviewed evidence considers IPS procedure, additional diagnostic yield, and safety.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2.1 Protocol and technical standards
document_sections.content: Only two category II studies and one category III study assessed IPS procedures. Among 45 patients with a photoparoxysmal response (PPR), 24.4% showed it only when closing the eyes during IPS. Another study found responses in 8.0% (21/263) of children; 45% of responses appeared after 9 seconds, supporting stimulation for 10 or more seconds at each frequency. In photosensitive patients, the frequency-related photosensitivity range reported as 2560 Hz was significantly higher, and maximal, with “eyes open with diffuser” than with “eyes open”, “eyes closed”, or “eye closure” (p=0.0002). Earlier EEG guidelines incorporated a European expert-panel recommendation on photic-stimulation methods.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2.2 Yield of intermittent photic stimulation
document_sections.content: A category I study found that IPS disclosed generalized epileptiform discharges absent before stimulation in 1.5% (79/5383) of patients and supplied the only useful information—epileptiform discharges or epileptic or non-epileptic seizures—in 2.3% (122/5383). Category II studies found generalized discharges as the sole epileptiform activity in 0.68% (5/732) of EEGs and abnormalities occurring only with IPS in 5.3% (12/226). In comparison, 0.32% (44/13658) of Air Force applicants had abnormalities induced only by IPS. A category III study reported that IPS elicited the sole epileptiform abnormalities in 30.5% of patients aged 14 – 17 years with genetic (idiopathic) generalized epilepsy. Another category III study found added yield versus baseline in 3.7% (15/406) of newly diagnosed epilepsy patients; repeating IPS after an initially normal EEG detected activity in 3.0% (5/164), with greatest yield below 20 years of age and in generalized seizures. A category II study reported photoparoxysmal responses in 2.3% of 2,888 consecutive recordings and 10% of patients with epilepsy. A category III study reported photosensitivity type 1 to 4 in 74% of patients with epilepsy and generalized tonic clonic seizures on awakening, 56% with juvenile absence epilepsy, 50% with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, 44% with childhood absence epilepsy, 23% with childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, and 16% with symptomatic/cryptogenic epilepsy. Among photosensitivity reactions, type 4 was significantly more frequent in genetic generalized epilepsy (59%) than in childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes (38%). A nationwide Great Britain study estimated annual incidence of epilepsy patients showing generalized spike-and-wave discharges with IPS at their first EEG at roughly 1.1 per 100,000, or approximately 2% of new epilepsy cases.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2.3 Safety
document_sections.content: A nationwide UK category I study attributed seizures to IPS in 0.72% (39/5383) of patients, including generalized tonic clonic seizures in 0.04%; IPS also provoked psychogenic non-epileptic seizures in 0.9% (49/5383). Two category II studies found seizures occurring exclusively with IPS in 0.53% (1/189) and 0.68% (5/732). Among Air Force applicants, IPS caused epileptic seizures in 0.068% (4/5,893), three out of four being generalized tonic-clonic seizures. A category III study found significantly more psychogenic non-epileptic seizures after patients with psychogenic seizures alone or alongside epileptic seizures were informed about possible seizure induction. In the informed group, IPS provoked such events in 17.6% (6/34); two thirds (4/6) occurred only during IPS.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3 Other provocation methods
document_sections.content: Evidence did not support routine use of activation methods other than hyperventilation and IPS. Other methods were principally considered for genetic generalized epilepsies with a reflex trait or focal-onset epilepsies with a specific seizure trigger. Three category III studies in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and two in genetic generalized epilepsies compared cognitive tasks with deprivation, IPS, and hyperventilation. Cognitive protocols lasted at least 15 minutes and typically over 30 minutes. Cognitive tasks might yield more than hyperventilation or IPS, but not more than sleep. Two studies observed no seizures during cognitive testing; three did. In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, cognitive tasks provoked more myoclonia than conventional methods. Other category II-III investigations of visual patterns in unselected children aged four to 12 years and pediatric patients with visually induced seizures, and of olfactory stimuli in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, found no increased diagnostic utility for routine EEG.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4 Recommendation
document_sections.content: Evidence for hyperventilation provoking epileptiform discharges is moderate despite study limitations and rests on three consistent category I observational studies. Evidence for photic and other stimulation is low. Modified Delphi consensus suggests including hyperventilation, photic stimulation, and baseline eyes-open and eyes-closed recording in routine or sleep EEG unless contraindicated. Asking patients to blink and open and close their eyes documents artifacts and can reveal eye-closure sensitivity. EEG should be tailored with simple stimuli such as touch, sudden noises, or reading difficult text aloud when these are known seizure triggers. Patients and caregivers should receive advance information about potential benefits and harms of activation, particularly seizures and possible loss of driving permission. Such information may itself increase non-epileptic seizures; patients have the right to know they may decline activation. The EEG technician is responsible for safety and recording quality and must monitor only one recording continuously. Patients should never be left alone and should not remain solely under a parent’s or guardian’s observation for more than a few minutes. Standardized testing during seizures is advisable; simplified versions of ILAE and UK long-term video-EEG procedures are suggested in Table 5. For a possible absence seizure with generalized spike-and-wave discharge lasting longer than 3-4 seconds, the suggested ILAE task-force approach is to give simple commands or words from discharge onset and throughout the event, observe spontaneous responses, and ask afterward what was said. In adults, IPS is suggested before hyperventilation near EEG onset, separated by at least 3 minutes. When the referral concerns genetic generalized epilepsy, activations are advisable at the end because seizures are more likely. IPS tends to increase vigilance and impede sleep, whereas hyperventilation has the opposite effect; consequently, for pediatric sleep EEG, hyperventilation is suggested at the beginning and IPS at the end.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4.1 Hyperventilation protocol
document_sections.content: Patients are instructed to breathe deeply 15-30 times/minute for at least three minutes. A windmill may help children breathe adequately. Perioral or finger numbness or tingling can occur and alone does not justify stopping. The technician should encourage the patient and judge respiratory effort as adequate or inadequate. Recording two minutes of awake EEG afterward is preferable for every patient group. Contraindications are sickle cell disease or trait, Moya-Moya disease and syndrome, cerebrovascular malformations including aneurysms, cerebrovascular events in the last three months, raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias or other severe cardiac disorders, severe pulmonary disorders, and pregnancy. Preferably, referring physicians should have a contraindication list for reporting relevant conditions. At minimum, particularly if referral and EEG are separated in time, the technician should ask patients about contraindications and record their answers.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4.2 Intermittent photic stimulation protocol
document_sections.content: IPS is suggested according to the cited ILAE photic-stimulation methodology. Repeating it during the same EEG is unnecessary if its result is unequivocal. Pregnancy is a contraindication because seizure risk is high.

document_sections.heading: 3.6 Conclusions
document_sections.content: Routine and sleep EEG have an established diagnostic role in epilepsy. Overall evidence quality for their recording standards is low, an important limitation. The document combines available evidence with expert-consensus recording standards. Although conditional, its recommendations offer feasible standards for new laboratories and a basis for established laboratories to reassess protocols. Further methodological development and diagnostic-accuracy research are needed.
